explain.say: On 26 June 1945, in San Francisco, delegates of fifty nations signed the United Nations Charter, while war still raged in the Pacific. Its first words are we the peoples. Poland signed soon after, making fifty-one founding members. Look at the timeline from the failed League to the new UN.

explain.say: Why try again? See the comparison. The League of Nations, from 1920, never had the United States, needed every member to agree, and had no army of its own. It failed to stop Japan in Manchuria and Italy in Ethiopia in the 1930s. The UN's planners wanted a body with teeth. Which League flaw would you fix first?

draw.name: x-compare
draw.verdict: Built to fix the League's flaws.

explain.say: Now the map. Plans were drafted at Dumbarton Oaks in Washington in 1944. At Yalta in February 1945, Roosevelt, Churchill and Stalin agreed that the great powers would hold a veto. The Charter was signed in San Francisco, and the UN made its home in New York, while the League's old palace in Geneva became a UN office. Why might the great powers insist on a veto?

Look at the network. Every member has one vote in the General Assembly. The Security Council can order sanctions or authorise force, but its five permanent members, the USA, Russia, which took the Soviet seat, Britain, France and China, can each veto a decision. The Assembly also elects the World Court's judges. Can you see why the veto keeps powers in, yet can freeze the Council?

nodes.label: Security Council
nodes.ask: Why do five countries have a veto?

explain.say: Here is real growth. The UN began with 51 members, reached 99 by 1960 as African states won independence, and has 193 today since South Sudan joined in 2011. Decolonisation reshaped the world body. Brilliant work. Challenge: argue for or against changing who holds a Security Council veto.

faq.q: Why was the United Nations created?
faq.a: To keep international peace after the Second World War, with the great powers inside it, and to promote cooperation on economic, social and human rights issues. Its Charter was signed in San Francisco on 26 June 1945 and came into force on 24 October 1945.
asks: What does the UN Charter say?

faq.q: How is the UN different from the League of Nations?
faq.a: The League, from 1920, lacked the United States, needed unanimous decisions and had no means to enforce them, and failed in the 1930s. The UN included the USA and USSR, uses majority voting in the Assembly, and its Security Council can authorise sanctions and military force.
asks: Why did the League of Nations fail?

faq.q: Why do five countries have a veto?
faq.a: At Yalta in 1945 the big Allied powers agreed that they would each hold a veto in the Security Council. The aim was to keep them committed to the UN, unlike the League; the cost is that one of them can block action. The five are the USA, Russia, Britain, France and China.
asks: Who are the permanent members of the Security Council?

faq.q: What does the General Assembly do?
faq.a: Every member state has one vote in the General Assembly. It debates world issues, passes resolutions, sets the budget, admits members on the Security Council's advice and elects non-permanent Council members and World Court judges.
asks: How does voting work in the UN?

faq.q: How many members does the UN have?
faq.a: It began with 51 members in 1945 and grew quickly with decolonisation, to 99 by 1960. It has 193 member states today, the newest being South Sudan in 2011.
asks: Which is the newest UN member?

facts: The UN Charter was signed in San Francisco on 26 June 1945.
The UN officially came into existence on 24 October 1945.
South Sudan became the 193rd UN member in 2011.

quiz.say: The UN grew from 51 members in 1945 to 193 today. How many joined after the founding?

wrong.1: 193 is today's total, including the founders.

quiz.say: Which UN body can authorise the use of force?
quiz.why: Under the Charter, the Security Council can order sanctions and authorise military action.

wrong.1: The General Assembly can recommend but not order force.
wrong.2: The World Court settles legal disputes between states.
